title: 1930s–1950s: Universal Monsters
thematicFocus: Gothic escapism, romanticized monsters, external threats, nuclear anxiety.
culturalContext: Born during the Great Depression and World War II, horror allowed audiences to project real-world anxieties onto fantastical creatures. Later, Cold War nuclear fears manifested in giant monster cinema.

title: 1960s–1970s: Psychological Shift
thematicFocus: Real-world violence, domestic terror, loss of institutional trust, female autonomy.
culturalContext: Civil rights unrest, the Vietnam War, and the decay of the nuclear family shifted horror into domestic spaces. Monsters became human neighbors, masked killers, or bodily threats.

title: 1980s: Slasher Boom & The Satanic Panic
thematicFocus: Franchise morality plays, practical gore, censorship, home video explosion.
culturalContext: The rise of VHS expanded horror consumption, spurring mass-market slasher franchises while conservative movements and Satanic Panic led to heavy censorship.

title: 1990s: Postmodern Revival
thematicFocus: Self-awareness, meta-commentary, genre deconstruction, structural cynicism.
culturalContext: Over-saturation of 80s sequels caused horror to become self-conscious. Meta-horror subverted classic slasher rules for audiences raised on the genre.

title: 2000s: Extreme Realism & Torture Cinema
thematicFocus: Post-9/11 anxiety, surveillance, visceral vulnerability, techno-dread.
culturalContext: Post-9/11 sociopolitical anxiety and 24-hour news coverage fueled claustrophobic violence, alongside techno-dread remakes of J-horror.

title: 2010s–Present: Blockbuster Haunted Houses & Elevated Horror
thematicFocus: Cinematic universes vs. grief, trauma, social inequality, and auteur dread.
culturalContext: The modern era split into studio-driven jump-scare franchises and indie elevated horror using horror conventions to explore grief and generational trauma.
